mcqs.question: Why can't you determine the execution order of two independently registered event handlers just by reading the source code?
options: Because the order is determined by when the real-world events actually occur, not by the position of the handler registrations in the code
Because JavaScript randomizes handler execution order for security reasons
Because handlers are always executed in reverse registration order
Because event-driven code cannot be read or reasoned about at all
mcqs.explanation: Event-driven execution order is dictated by when events actually happen, not by the sequence handlers appear in the file — that's the defining inversion of control from imperative code. There's no randomization or reverse-order rule, and the code is very much reasoned about, just not by reading top to bottom.

mcqs.question: In a single-threaded event loop, what determines which handler runs next when two unrelated events (a click and a timer tick) are both pending?
options: Whichever handler was defined first in the source file
The order the events were queued/dequeued by the loop, since the handlers have no caller/callee relationship to each other
The handlers run simultaneously on separate threads
The one with fewer lines of code always runs first
mcqs.explanation: The event loop dequeues events in the order they were queued and runs each handler to completion before checking the queue again — there's no call relationship between independent handlers to determine order. Source-file position, line count, and simultaneous execution on separate threads don't apply to a single-threaded loop.

mcqs.question: What does pub/sub give you that a direct function call between a publisher and a specific subscriber does not?
options: Faster execution, since pub/sub always runs on a separate optimized thread
Guaranteed delivery order across every subscriber
Automatic conversion of synchronous code into asynchronous code
Decoupling — the publisher can emit an event without knowing how many subscribers exist or who they are, letting new subscribers be added later with no change to the publisher
mcqs.explanation: The core payoff of pub/sub is decoupling the publisher from the number and identity of subscribers, unlike a direct call which hardcodes exactly who gets invoked. It makes no performance or threading guarantee and doesn't magically make code asynchronous, and delivery order across independent subscribers is not guaranteed by the pattern itself.

mcqs.question: Why doesn't wrapping a chain of nested callbacks in a normal try/catch reliably catch an error thrown inside an inner callback?
options: Because try/catch only works on synchronous code, and errors thrown asynchronously inside an inner callback happen after the outer try/catch's synchronous execution has already completed
Because JavaScript disables exception handling inside any callback function
Because nested callbacks automatically swallow all errors silently by design
Because try/catch can only wrap a maximum of one function call
mcqs.explanation: A try/catch block only covers the synchronous execution within its scope; by the time an inner asynchronous callback runs and throws, the outer try/catch has already finished executing and can no longer catch anything, which is exactly the callback-hell error-propagation problem. Exceptions aren't disabled or silently swallowed, and there's no such call-depth limit.

mcqs.question: Why would you reach for a reactive stream library (like RxJS) instead of plain DOM event listeners when building autocomplete-as-you-type?
options: Plain DOM listeners cannot fire on keystroke events at all

Autocomplete needs to combine and transform multiple sources (keystrokes, debounce timing, network responses) declaratively, which reactive operators compose cleanly while plain listeners would require hand-written coordinating state
Reactive libraries are required by browsers to handle any text input
DOM events are deprecated in favor of reactive streams in modern browsers
mcqs.explanation: Autocomplete needs to compose several streams (keystrokes, a debounce delay, an async network call) and reactive operators express that composition declaratively, whereas plain listeners would need manually tracked timers and cancellation state. DOM keystroke events work fine on their own and are not deprecated; nothing requires a reactive library for basic text input.
